chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu Ubeyda, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who bought ostrich eggs for a man in Ihram, so the man in Ihram ate them. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is a ransom upon the one who bought it for the one in Ihram, and upon the one in Ihram is (also) a ransom.' I said, 'And what is upon both of them?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Upon the one not in Ihram is a penalty of the price of the eggs, for each egg being a Dirham; and upon the one in Ihram is the penalty, for each egg being a sheep.'
A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Abu Ubeyda – similar to it.

key_terms.مُحْرِمٍ: One in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj/Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for a person in Ihram eating ostrich eggs?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* elucidates the dual liability in Ihram expiations, distinguishing between the buyer's monetary compensation (one dirham per egg) and the pilgrim's sacrificial penalty (one sheep per egg). It reflects the Shia juristic principle that the act of consumption by the Muhrim incurs a heavier, animal-based fidyah, while the provider bears a lighter, value-based penalty, highlighting the nuanced allocation of responsibility in ritual purity laws.
